Solar power has become one of the most promising sources of clean energy in the world. A solar panel works by capturing sunlight and converting it into electricity through small cells made of silicon. Unlike fuels such as coal or oil, sunlight will never run out, and using it produces no smoke that pollutes the air. In countries with strong sunshine for most of the year, solar panels can supply electricity to homes, schools, and clinics that are far from any city power line. Although the panels can be expensive to buy at first, they cost very little to run afterwards, because the sun provides the fuel for free. For this reason, many governments now encourage families and businesses to install them.

Question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Solar power is a clean and useful source of energy worth using.
Coal and oil are cheaper than solar panels in every country.
Silicon is the only material used to build modern houses.
City power lines are always better than solar panels.
questions.explanation: The passage as a whole presents solar power as a clean, promising, and practical energy source.

When people in a town all want to buy the same thing, the price of that thing often rises. This happens because sellers notice the strong demand and know that buyers are willing to pay more. Imagine that a sudden festival brings thousands of visitors to a small market. Suddenly everyone wants bread, fruit, and bottled water at the same time. The sellers have only a limited amount to offer, so they raise their prices, and the goods are sold to those who can afford them. When the festival ends and the visitors leave, demand falls again, and prices usually return to their normal level. Economists call this simple relationship the law of supply and demand, and it helps explain why the cost of everyday goods can change so quickly from one week to the next.

Question: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How festivals are organised in small towns.
Why prices change according to supply and demand.
The best kinds of food to sell at a market.
How visitors choose which town to travel to.
questions.explanation: The passage uses the festival example to explain how supply and demand cause prices to change.

Long before modern roads existed, traders carried goods across the deserts of northern Africa on the backs of camels. These long journeys, sometimes lasting many weeks, linked distant towns into a single network of trade. Camels were ideal for the task because they could travel for days with little water and could carry heavy loads of salt, gold, and cloth across burning sands. Along the routes, small settlements grew into busy markets where merchants from different regions met to exchange not only goods but also ideas, languages, and beliefs. In this way, trade did far more than make a few people wealthy. It spread knowledge of distant places, encouraged the learning of new languages, and helped cultures that had never met to influence one another. The desert, once seen only as a barrier, became a bridge between peoples.

Question: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Camels are the strongest animals found in the desert.
Desert trade connected distant peoples and spread goods and ideas.
Salt and gold were once worthless in northern Africa.
Modern roads have completely replaced desert trade routes.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasises that trade across the desert linked peoples and spread both goods and ideas.

Some people argue that students learn best when examinations are removed entirely from schools. They claim that tests cause needless fear and reward memorising over real understanding. While it is true that exams can create anxiety, removing them completely would do more harm than good. Examinations give students a clear goal to work towards and a fair way to measure what they have learned. Without them, hard-working learners would have no proof of their effort, and lazy ones could pass unnoticed. The real problem is not the existence of exams but the way some are designed. A well-made test should ask students to think, not merely to repeat facts. Therefore, instead of abolishing examinations, schools should improve them, making sure they reward genuine understanding. In this way, the benefits of testing can be kept while its worst effects are reduced.

Question: What is the author's main argument in this passage?
options: Examinations should be removed from all schools immediately.
Examinations should be improved rather than abolished.
Students who feel anxious should not be allowed to take exams.
Memorising facts is the best way to succeed in school.
questions.explanation: The author argues against abolishing exams and instead calls for improving them so they reward real understanding.

The old fishermen of the village rose before the sun, when the sky was still the colour of ash. Among them was Kebede, whose hands were rough as bark from years of pulling nets. Each morning he pushed his small wooden boat onto the grey water and rowed until the shore became a thin line behind him. The sea, he often said, was neither cruel nor kind; it simply was, and a wise man learned to read its moods the way others read a book. On calm days he sang quietly to himself, but when dark clouds gathered he fell silent and watched the waves with patient, knowing eyes. The younger men laughed at his caution, yet they always returned safely when they followed him. Kebede asked the sea for nothing it could not give, and in return it had let him grow old.

Question: What does the passage mainly reveal about Kebede?
options: He is a wealthy man who owns many large boats.
He is an experienced fisherman who deeply understands the sea.
He is afraid of the water and rarely goes fishing.
He dislikes the younger men and refuses to help them.
questions.explanation: The passage portrays Kebede as a seasoned fisherman who reads the sea's moods wisely and is respected by others.
